$comment: ACKNOWLEDGED SCHEMA DRIFT between production and what supabase/migrations/ produces.
The build reads this file. Anything NOT listed here fails the drift check.
That is the point: it turns the drift inventory from a document nobody reads
into a list the build reads.
Every entry carries four things and an entry missing any of them is incomplete:
object        what differs, precisely enough to match a catalog row
direction     which side is which, because it decides who has to change
why_tolerated why this is not a red today
resolves_when what would let the entry be DELETED. An entry with no exit is
a permanent exemption pretending to be a temporary one.
Established by catalog diff on 2026-09-24: production read via the management
API, the migration side read from a stack CI raised from these files. Compared
as two catalogs, never as a catalog against a reading of SQL.
ALREADY RESOLVED and deliberately absent, so nobody re-adds them:
household_members 'Users can join as themselves'  - dropped in production
households 'Users can create a household they own' - dropped in production
categories trg_category_visibility_owner + its function - added to production
(verified by hash against the migration-built catalog, not by presence)
FUNCTION COMPARISON MUST BE DONE TWICE, AND THE CHECK DOES BOTH:
raw        md5(pg_get_functiondef) - exact, but flags comment-only edits
normalised comments stripped + whitespace collapsed - flags BEHAVIOUR
A mismatch is classified from the pair: raw differs + normalised matches is
COSMETIC; normalised differs is BEHAVIOURAL and is never allowlisted without
a stated reason. Stripping `--` is not free - a string literal containing `--`
would be corrupted by it, so the normalised form is used only to CLASSIFY a
mismatch, never as the sole basis for calling two functions equal.
FIRST-CLASS, NOT A TEST OF THE CHECK. If either catalog returns fewer
objects than these floors, the check FAILS HARD rather than reporting
'no drift'. A diff over two empty catalogs is silent agreement, which is
the exact failure mode hit three times in the week this file was written:
no-floating-promises reporting 0 because nothing invoked it, an RLS
mutation that would have passed against the wrong database, and a clock
parameter no caller passed.
Floors are set below current values so ordinary growth does not trip them,
and far enough above zero that an empty or half-read catalog cannot pass.
FLOORS MUST BE DERIVED FROM THE QUERY THAT ACTUALLY RUNS. column_grant_entries
was first set to 1200 from information_schema.column_privileges, which counts
privileges IMPLIED by table grants. The check reads pg_attribute.attacl, which
holds only EXPLICIT column grants - 12 of them here (hp-8's user_profiles
re-grant and the insights engagement columns). The floor was carried over from
a different measurement, and the first real run correctly refused to proceed.
That is the floors working, not the floors being wrong to have.

allowed_drift.object: policy public.insights "Service can insert insights for users" (INSERT)
allowed_drift.why_tolerated: Production is STRICTER and correct. The migration's policy is WITH CHECK (true), which would let any authenticated user insert an arbitrary insight row for anyone. Removing it from production was right; the migration is what is wrong.
allowed_drift.resolves_when: A migration drops this policy, bringing the file up to production. Then delete this entry.
match: service can insert insights for users

allowed_drift.object: policy public.insights "Users and services can delete insights" (DELETE)
allowed_drift.why_tolerated: Production is STRICTER. The migration's USING clause is (auth.uid() = user_id OR auth.uid() IS NULL), and the IS NULL arm makes it permissive for any unauthenticated context. Insights are deleted by the service role, which bypasses RLS and needs no policy.
allowed_drift.resolves_when: A migration drops this policy. Then delete this entry.
match: users and services can delete insights

allowed_drift.object: policy public.wishlist_items "Users can update their own wishlist items" (UPDATE) - WITH CHECK predicate differs
allowed_drift.why_tolerated: Production's WITH CHECK also validates that category_id belongs to the user and is an expense category; the migration's checks only (auth.uid() = user_id). Production prevents pointing a wishlist item at someone else's category.
allowed_drift.resolves_when: A migration updates the policy to match production's predicate. Then delete this entry.
match: users can update their own wishlist items

allowed_drift.object: function public.seed_user_categories(uuid) - body AND proconfig differ
allowed_drift.why_tolerated: NOT ORDINARY DRIFT, and must not sit here as though it were. Production has search_path pinned to public; the migrations leave it UNPINNED. So applying the migrations forward would REGRESS part of migration 038's security-advisor hardening pass. This single entry disqualifies the obvious reconciliation plan - 'just apply the migrations forward' - and it is the first thing anyone will reach for.
allowed_drift.resolves_when: A migration recreates seed_user_categories WITH `SET search_path = public`, bringing the file up to production rather than the reverse. Only then delete this entry. Never resolve it by applying the migration version to production.

allowed_drift.object: column default on every table's `id`: production renders extensions.uuid_generate_v4(), the migrations render uuid_generate_v4()
allowed_drift.direction: ENVIRONMENT DIFFERENCE, not application schema. Same function, different schema qualification.
allowed_drift.why_tolerated: 23 findings from ONE cause, and a uniform delta across independent objects is the signature of a systematic difference rather than 23 independent ones. 001_initial_schema.sql says `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "uuid-ossp";` with no schema, so locally it lands in public and pg_get_expr renders the default unqualified. Supabase-managed projects place extensions in the `extensions` schema, so production renders it qualified. The generated value is identical; only the rendered qualification differs. Deliberately NOT normalised away in the comparator: stripping a schema prefix from a default expression would also mask a genuine change of default, and this is narrow enough to state as an exception instead.
allowed_drift.resolves_when: 001 is changed to `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "uuid-ossp" WITH SCHEMA extensions;` so the local stack matches production — which needs the extensions schema to exist locally first, so it is a real change rather than a one-liner. Then delete this entry. Note the match tokens are specific to uuid_generate_v4, so a default changed to anything else still fails.

$comment: NOT SUPPRESSIONS. allowed_drift holds only entries that stop a HARD FAILURE.
These are investigated findings needing no suppression - kept so the
investigation is not repeated, and separated so 'anything not on the list
fails' stays true of allowed_drift alone.

entries.object: functions public.patch_user_preferences(jsonb) and public.record_feature_activity(date) - pg_get_functiondef hashes differ
entries.direction: COSMETIC ONLY - production's stored body lacks inline `--` comments that the migration files contain. Logic identical.
entries.why_tolerated: INVESTIGATED AND RESOLVED AS BENIGN, not deferred. Normalising both bodies the same way - strip `--` comments, collapse whitespace, lowercase - yields byte-identical text on both sides: patch_user_preferences 0e69c328b720497ff948a4cffa7650e8 (464 chars) and record_feature_activity 4982299f0a6ec3308ce23415b55b0e15 (492 chars), matching production exactly. Both also agree on search_path and on SECURITY INVOKER. There is no behavioural difference; production was created from a comment-free version of the same text.
entries.resolves_when: Re-running each migration's CREATE OR REPLACE against production converges the stored text. Idempotent and behaviour-neutral, so it can ride along with any future migration. Then delete this entry.
entries.$note: A FIRST ATTEMPT AT THIS COMPARISON REPORTED 'BODIES GENUINELY DIFFER' AND WAS WRONG. The Python side called .strip() and the SQL side did not, so leading/trailing newlines collapsed to spaces on one side only - both functions came out off by exactly 2 characters, which is what gave it away. A uniform tiny delta across independent objects is a signature of the comparison being broken, not the objects differing.

entries.object: column public.detected_subscriptions.currency, and the 8 column-grant entries consequent on it
entries.outcome: RESOLVED 2026-09-24 - migration 20260924110000 applied. Verified: character varying(3), NOT NULL, default 'EUR'; table at 10 columns; column-grant entries 72 -> 80 as predicted.
entries.note: Deleted from allowed_drift the same day it was applied, per the rule that a resolved item left in an allowlist becomes permanent noise.

$comment: Conditions the check deliberately does NOT cover, recorded so they are not
mistaken for things it watches. These are NOT in allowed_drift, because every
entry there must be matchable against a catalog record - an unmatchable entry
would sit permanently in the 'unmatched' hygiene report and make that report
meaningless, which is how a signal becomes noise.

entries.object: supabase_migrations.schema_migrations - 20260924100000 is NOT recorded although its effects are present in production
entries.why_tolerated: The security fix was applied as raw SQL rather than through the migration pipeline, so production has the change without the record. Harmless for correctness here because every statement in it is idempotent (DROP POLICY IF EXISTS, CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION, DROP+CREATE TRIGGER), so a later push re-applying it is a no-op.
entries.resolves_when: The version is inserted into schema_migrations, or the migration is applied through the pipeline so it records itself. Then delete this entry.
entries.$note: Recorded here because it means 'which migrations has production applied' is unreliable in a SECOND way, independent of schema drift. 012 is recorded and did nothing; 20260924100000 did something and is not recorded. The ledger cannot be trusted in either direction, which is an argument for the drift check comparing CATALOGS rather than consulting the ledger at all.

$comment: THE AXES ON WHICH THE LOCAL STACK CAN DIFFER FROM PRODUCTION, enumerated once
on 2026-09-24 so the class stops being discovered one instance at a time.
'The RLS suite tests a different database from production' had by then been
true THREE times for three unrelated causes - a missing policy, a missing
trigger, and a different Postgres major version. Each was found separately and
each by accident, and accident is not a control.
affects_rls_suite says whether the axis can change what the isolation tests
PROVE, which is the only question that matters about it.

axes.affects_rls_suite: YES. Privilege sets, catalog view shapes and behaviour all change between majors - PG17 adding MAINTAIN is what exposed the original mismatch.
axes.checked: HARD ASSERTION. Mismatch or absence fails the build, with both versions named.

axes.affects_rls_suite: YES, totally. RLS off makes every policy decorative.
axes.checked: reported as an environment axis; a difference would be visible immediately. Per-table relrowsecurity is ALSO compared as an RLS record and hard-fails.

axes.affects_rls_suite: POSSIBLY. Text ordering and comparison differ between ICU and libc, and comparisons appear in policy predicates - though this schema's predicates compare uuid and boolean, not text.
axes.checked: reported as DBPROPS. Not a hard failure because it has never differed and a change would be deliberate.

axes.affects_rls_suite: TimeZone could, via date bucketing in a predicate. Encoding and DateStyle do not.

axes.status: DIFFER: authenticator session_preload_libraries is 'safeupdate' in production and 'supautils, safeupdate' locally; the local stack sets app.settings.jwt_secret and production does not.
axes.affects_rls_suite: search_path YES in principle - a SECURITY DEFINER function without a pinned search_path resolves differently. Migration 038 pinned every one, which is what makes this currently harmless. The two observed differences do not.
axes.checked: reported as ROLESETTING, read from pg_db_role_setting. NOT from pg_settings: that reflects the CONNECTING ROLE, and comparing production-as-schema_reader against local-as-superuser produced two differences that said nothing about either database. Secret-shaped values are redacted to an md5 so a change is still detected without publishing the value.

axes.status: DIFFER: hypopg 1.4.1 and index_advisor 0.2.0 exist in production only.
axes.affects_rls_suite: NO. Both are Supabase diagnostic extensions with no policy or data involvement. A version difference in pgcrypto or uuid-ossp WOULD matter, because it changes generated values - and that had never been checked before this.
axes.checked: reported as EXTENSION, with version and schema.

axes.status: DIFFERS: uuid-ossp is in `extensions` in production and in `public` locally.
axes.affects_rls_suite: NO. Same function, same generated value; only the rendered default qualification differs.
axes.checked: allowlisted as uuid-ossp-extension-schema, with a resolves_when.

axes.affects_rls_suite: NO - the suite seeds its own users and rows, which is why it can run against an empty stack at all.
axes.checked: NOT CHECKED, and must not be. The production reader is a grantless role that cannot read a single row, which is the property that makes putting its credential in CI acceptable.

axes.status: DIVERGES in both directions - 012 recorded and inert, 20260924100000 effective and unrecorded.
axes.checked: DELIBERATELY NOT. See known_conditions_not_checked; the check compares catalogs precisely because the ledger cannot be trusted either way.
